1.title: The First Taking of Jerusalem
1.context: Daniel was deported in the first of three takings of Jerusalem, in 605 BC, years before the city and temple were destroyed in 586. Babylon's policy was to absorb the best of conquered peoples into its own court service.
1.question: What has God placed in your hands, like Daniel's training, that was meant for a place you did not choose?

1.title: A Mind Made Up at the Table
1.context: The king's food was likely rich fare that included meats forbidden by Israel's food laws and meat and wine first offered to Babylon's gods. Daniel's resolution is stated before any pressure arrives.
1.question: Where have you had to decide a line in advance, before the moment of pressure came?

1.title: A Ten-Day Test
1.context: Daniel's proposal put the decision on visible evidence and left it in the steward's hands, a pattern of firm conviction carried with courtesy that runs through his whole career.
1.question: How do you hold a conviction firmly without making an enemy of the person in front of you?

1.title: Knowledge as a Gift
1.context: The text credits the four men's learning to God directly, and singles out Daniel's insight into visions and dreams, the gift the rest of the book is built on.
1.question: What ability in your life do you most need to remember is a gift rather than an achievement?

1.title: Ten Times Better
1.context: Chapter 1 ends by measuring Daniel's career in advance: he remains in royal service until Cyrus, the Persian king who would conquer Babylon and let the exiles go home.
1.question: Who in your life has quietly outlasted every regime change around them? What kept them standing?

2.title: The Dream No One Could Tell
2.context: Kings in the ancient world treated dreams as messages from the gods, and Babylon kept a professional guild to interpret them. Nebuchadnezzar's demand to be told the dream itself tested whether the guild had any real access to heaven. The text notes at verse 4 that the court answered in Aramaic; the book's original runs in Aramaic from here through chapter 7.
2.question: When have you been asked for something that was simply beyond human ability to deliver?

2.title: Discretion, Tact, and Time
2.context: Arioch commanded the king's guard. Daniel's approach, asking why the decree was so harsh and then requesting time from the king himself, stopped an execution already in motion.
2.question: What situation in front of you needs your first move to be a question rather than a reaction?

2.title: The Mystery in the Night
2.context: The four friends' prayer is the first recorded prayer in Daniel, and it is communal: Daniel carries the answer, but the asking was shared with the three men whose lives were also on the list.
2.question: Who are the people you bring an impossible matter to, before you bring it anywhere else?

2.title: He Removes Kings and Establishes Them
2.context: Daniel's hymn is spoken before he knows the dream's content matters to anyone but the condemned. Its themes, God changing times and seasons and revealing deep things, govern the whole book.
2.question: What would it change in you to bless God before the answer is used, rather than after it works?

2.title: Not Because I Have More Wisdom
2.context: Daniel's disclaimer is precise: the astrologers were right that no human could do this, and the revelation says nothing about Daniel's superiority, only about God's purpose for the king.
2.question: Where are you tempted to let a gift God gave you be read as proof that you are more than you are?

3.title: A Great and Dazzling Statue
3.context: The statue's metals descend in value from gold to clay while its strength peaks at iron. Daniel interprets the figure as a sequence of kingdoms, but names only the first, Nebuchadnezzar's own.
3.question: What impressive thing in your world is built of mixed materials that cannot hold together?

3.title: The Stone Cut Without Hands
3.context: Threshing floors were hilltop places where wind carried chaff away from grain. The stone's growth into a mountain filling the earth is the dream's final image, and Daniel's interpretation ties it to a kingdom God sets up.
3.question: What small, unhuman-made beginning have you watched become something no one could have built?

3.title: You Are That Head of Gold
3.context: Daniel tells the most powerful man on earth that his sovereignty is a gift from the God of heaven. Which later kingdoms fill the other metals is a question interpreters have answered differently; the text itself leaves them unnamed.
3.question: How does hearing that your place is a gift, rather than a conquest, change how you hold it?

3.title: A Kingdom That Will Never Be Destroyed
3.context: Iron and clay is the dream's picture of a divided kingdom: strong and brittle at once, its peoples mixed but not holding. Against it stands the one kingdom in the dream that no successor replaces.
3.question: Where do you need to remember that what God sets up is not at the mercy of what men mix together?

3.title: The God of Gods and Lord of Kings
3.context: Nebuchadnezzar's homage and confession are remarkable from a pagan king, and Daniel's first act in office is to have his three friends appointed with him, the men who had prayed through the night at his side.
3.question: Who prayed with you in a hard night and should share in what came of it?

4.title: Ninety Feet of Gold
4.context: The statue stood on the plain of Dura in Babylon's province. Its proportions, sixty cubits by six, are tall and narrow, more pillar than figure. The dedication gathered the empire's whole administration into one act of worship.
4.question: What does the pressure to join in look like in your world, when everyone is summoned and the music starts?

4.title: We Have No Need to Answer You
4.context: The three friends' answer holds two things at once: confidence that God is able to deliver, and refusal to make deliverance the condition of obedience. Daniel is not mentioned in this chapter, and the text gives no explanation for his absence.
4.question: What would you still refuse to do even if you knew God might not rescue you from the cost?

4.title: Four Men in the Fire
4.context: Nebuchadnezzar describes the fourth figure as looking like a son of the gods, and afterward says God sent His angel. The text keeps the king's own descriptions and lets them stand.
4.question: When has help arrived in a form you only recognized afterward for what it was?

4.title: No Smell of Fire
4.context: The inventory of what the fire did not touch is detailed: hair, robes, even smell. The only thing burned was the rope that bound them, and the king's blessing names trust as the reason for the deliverance.
4.question: What has a hard season burned away in you that turned out to be only what was binding you?

4.title: No Other God Who Can Deliver
4.context: The king's decree protects the three men's God across the empire. The chapter that began with a command to worship gold ends with the gold-builder praising the God of the men who refused.
4.question: Where have you seen a stand taken quietly outlast the power that demanded it bend?

5.title: A Letter to All the Earth
5.context: Chapter 4 is framed as Nebuchadnezzar's own public letter, the only chapter in Daniel written as a king's document. Its opening doxology is spoken by the king from the far side of the events he is about to confess.
5.question: What would you write to everyone if you had to publish the story of your own humbling?

5.title: The Dream Comes Back
5.context: Daniel's Babylonian name Belteshazzar is used throughout this chapter, and the king explains his trust in him: the spirit of the holy gods is in him, and no mystery baffles him.
5.question: Why do you think the king kept Daniel last, after his own guild had failed again?

5.title: A Tree in the Midst of the Land
5.context: Watchers are heavenly beings who carry out God's decrees. The decree's stated purpose is public and universal: so that the living will know the Most High rules the kingdom of mankind.
5.question: The decree says heaven's purpose is that the living will know who rules. What has taught you that lesson best?

5.title: You, O King, Are That Tree
5.context: Daniel delivers the worst interpretation in the empire to the king's face, and the dream's mercy is in the stump: banded with iron and bronze, left in the ground, a kingdom kept for a king who will acknowledge heaven.
5.question: What stump in your life, cut down but not uprooted, might be heaven's way of keeping something for you?

5.title: Break Away from Your Sins
5.context: Daniel's counsel is unique in the book: he urges the king to answer heaven's sentence with repentance and mercy to the oppressed, and holds out a perhaps of extended prosperity.
5.question: What counsel would you give a powerful friend if you loved them more than you feared them?

6.title: Babylon the Great
6.context: Twelve months separate the warning from its fulfillment. The king's rooftop sentence assigns the building, the power, and the glory to himself, the exact claims the dream had corrected.
6.question: What sentence do you catch yourself saying that leaves God out of your own story?

6.title: The Voice from Heaven
6.context: The sentence is fulfilled by announcement rather than invasion: no army takes Babylon, and the throne is left standing empty while its king is sent out among the beasts.
6.question: Where has God corrected you without destroying what He later gave back?

6.title: Hair Like Feathers, Nails Like Claws
6.context: The letter does not say who governed during the king's madness or how long the seven times lasted. Its interest is in the acknowledgment the decree was designed to produce.
6.question: What part of this story do you wish the text explained, and why do you think it leaves it untold?

6.title: My Sanity Was Restored to Me
6.context: The restoration begins with a look upward. Nebuchadnezzar's hymn is the confession of a man who once asked what god could deliver from his hands, now saying no one can restrain God's hand.
6.question: What has looking up, in the middle of a season you could not fix, restored in you?

6.title: Able to Humble Those Who Walk in Pride
6.context: The letter closes with the king publishing his humiliation to every nation as praise. Daniel's book preserves the testimony of Babylon's greatest king that the kingdom was never his.
6.question: What do you know about God's rule now that you could only have learned by being humbled?

7.title: The Vessels at the Feast
7.context: Belshazzar ruled Babylon as its king in its final years; outside the Bible he is known as the son of Nabonidus, governing in his father's place, which fits the offer of only third place in the kingdom later in the chapter. The temple vessels had been carried to Babylon in Daniel's own deportation era.
7.question: What holy thing have you seen treated as entertainment, and what did it cost?

7.title: The Fingers of a Human Hand
7.context: The writing appeared near the lampstand, where the light was strongest. The wise men's failure here is total: unlike earlier chapters, they cannot even read the words, let alone interpret them.
7.question: When has a small, quiet sign frightened you more than a loud threat would have?

7.title: The Queen Remembers Daniel
7.context: The queen, likely the queen mother, remembers what the court had forgotten: an aged exile from Nebuchadnezzar's reign. Daniel may have been in retirement, out of office for years by this night.
7.question: Whose memory of your faithfulness, kept by someone else, has opened a door for you?

7.title: You Knew All This
7.context: Daniel refuses the gifts before interpreting, and his sermon indicts Belshazzar not for ignorance but for knowledge unused: he had Nebuchadnezzar's whole story in front of him and learned nothing from it.
7.question: What story from your own family's past is heaven expecting you to learn from rather than repeat?

7.title: Weighed and Found Deficient
7.context: The inscription's words are weights and measures: numbered, weighed, divided. Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians that night in 539 BC, and Darius the Mede, named here and in chapter 6, received the kingdom at sixty-two.
7.question: If your life were weighed tonight, what would you want the scales to find more of?

8.title: No Charge Could Be Found
8.context: The new Persian administration kept Daniel at the top. His enemies' audit is a backhanded tribute: a lifetime in government with no negligence or corruption found, leaving his religion as the only attack surface.
8.question: What would your critics have to admit about you if they audited your whole record honestly?

8.title: Windows Open Toward Jerusalem
8.context: Daniel's prayer habit was public knowledge, three times daily at windows facing Jerusalem, the direction Solomon's dedication prayer had pointed exiles toward God. He changed nothing when the decree made it a capital crime.
8.question: What practice of yours would your enemies count on finding you at, and would they be right?

8.title: The King Trapped by His Own Decree
8.context: The law of the Medes and Persians was famous for being unchangeable, even by the king who signed it. Darius's words at the den's mouth show where his hope actually lay.
8.question: When have you had to live with the consequences of something you agreed to without thinking it through?

8.title: A Stone, a Seal, and a Sleepless King
8.context: The king fasts while Daniel sleeps among lions. Daniel's answer credits God's angel and states his innocence in two directions: before God, and before the king.
8.question: Who has kept a sleepless night over you, and what did their concern come to?

8.title: The Living God Who Endures Forever
8.context: Darius's decree is the third royal confession in the book, after Nebuchadnezzar's letter. Daniel prospering under Darius and Cyrus completes the promise of chapter 1's last verse.
8.question: Daniel served three empires without bending. What is the conviction that has carried you through every change of management in your life?

9.title: Visions in the Night
9.context: Chapter 7's vision is dated to Belshazzar's first year, earlier in story time than the feast of chapter 5. The book keeps its own order rather than the calendar's, and from here the dreams come to Daniel himself.
9.question: What is the difference for you between interpreting someone else's trouble and receiving a word of your own?

9.title: Lion, Bear, and Leopard
9.context: The first beast's transformation, wings torn off and a man's mind given, echoes Nebuchadnezzar's humbling and restoration. The vision does not name the kingdoms the beasts represent, and readers have traced them differently.
9.question: Which of these pictures of power, speed, appetite, or pride, feels most familiar from the world you watch?

9.title: The Little Horn with a Mouth
9.context: Iron appears again, now as teeth. The horn's distinguishing marks are eyes and speech: it watches and it boasts, the vision's smallest figure and its most arrogant.
9.question: Why do you think the vision makes arrogance, not size, the mark of the worst power?

9.title: The Ancient of Days Took His Seat
9.context: The court scene is the still center of the vision: thrones set, books opened, judgment conducted as a session rather than a battle. The beast's end takes a single verse once the court sits.
9.question: What does it do to your fears to picture judgment as a seated court with opened books?

9.title: One Like the Son of Man
9.context: The figure who comes with the clouds receives the everlasting dominion the beasts lose. Jesus would later take this title for Himself, which is how most Christian readers identify the figure; the vision itself lets him approach the throne unexplained.
9.question: Every kingdom in the dream ends except this one. What are you building your life on that will not pass away?

10.title: The Saints Will Receive the Kingdom
10.context: The interpretation's first summary is the promise the rest of the chapter will test: four kings arise from the earth, and the saints of the Most High receive the kingdom forever.
10.question: What does it mean to you that the kingdom is finally given to a people, not to another beast?

10.title: Waging War and Prevailing, Until
10.context: Daniel's second look adds the detail that the horn was prevailing against the saints, and the limit on it: until the Ancient of Days arrived and judgment was pronounced in the saints' favor.
10.question: Where do you need the word until today, in a situation where the wrong side is prevailing?

10.title: A Time, and Times, and Half a Time
10.context: The king is described by his speech against the Most High, his oppression of the saints, and his intent to change the appointed times and laws. The grant of time is measured and strange, a time, times, and half a time, and the text does not convert it into dates.
10.question: What appointed times and rhythms of worship would you refuse to let any power reschedule?

10.title: Given to the People, the Saints
10.context: The transfer of sovereignty is the chapter's destination: dominion taken from the horn is given to the saints, under a kingdom where all rulers serve and obey Him.
10.question: How does it shape your hope to know the end of the story is a people receiving a kingdom, not escaping a world?

10.title: I Kept the Matter to Myself
10.context: Daniel's postscript is honest about the cost of revelation: troubled thoughts and a pale face. He shares the dream in writing for us, but carried it alone in his own day.
10.question: What has God shown you that you have had to carry quietly for a long time?

11.title: A Ram Beside the Ulai
11.context: The vision sets Daniel in Susa, a Persian royal city, before Persia rules the world. Gabriel's interpretation will name the ram outright as the kings of Media and Persia, the only vision in the book whose symbols are identified in the text.
11.question: What is God showing you now whose meaning you will only understand from a later vantage point?

11.title: The Goat That Did Not Touch the Ground
11.context: The goat is Greece, its great horn the first king, Alexander, whose empire broke into four at his death. The little horn that rises later attacks the sanctuary and the daily sacrifice, events many readers connect with Antiochus IV in the second century BC; the text names none of these, only the vision and its interpretation.
11.question: Where have you seen truth flung to the ground and prospering, and how did you keep hold of it?

11.title: 2,300 Evenings and Mornings
11.context: The holy ones' question is how long, and the answer is a number, evenings and mornings, tied to the sanctuary's restoration. Readers have understood the figure in more than one way; the vision gives the number and the promise together.
11.question: What are you measuring in evenings and mornings right now, waiting for a sanctuary of your own to be restored?

11.title: Gabriel, Explain the Vision
11.context: Gabriel is the first angel named in Daniel, sent to teach rather than to rescue. His opening word frames the whole vision: it concerns the time of the end.
11.question: When has an explanation from heaven begun by telling you when a thing belongs, before telling you what it means?

11.title: Seal Up the Vision
11.context: The interpretation names Media, Persia, and Greece, then describes a king broken not by human hands. Daniel's response to receiving the meaning is exhaustion and days of illness, an honest record of what revelation cost him.
11.question: What truth have you been given that left you more confounded the longer you carried it?

12.title: Reading Jeremiah's Scroll
12.context: Daniel reads Jeremiah 25 and 29, where the seventy years of Jerusalem's desolation were promised and a future and hope attached to them. Daniel's own book is now the record of a man interpreting Scripture, not only dreams.
12.question: What promise in Scripture have you counted the years on, and what did the counting move you to do?

12.title: We Have Sinned and Done Wrong
12.context: Daniel's confession is entirely plural. The man in whose record no corruption could be found prays as a member of the people who rebelled, not as an exception to them.
12.question: Whose sins do you find it hardest to confess as your own people's, and therefore partly yours?

12.title: Righteousness Belongs to You, Shame to Us
12.context: The prayer's center sets two things side by side: God's righteousness in every disaster, and His compassion and forgiveness despite the rebellion that caused them. Daniel calls the catastrophe just while standing in its ruins.
12.question: Can you name a hard season where you could say God was righteous in all He did, even then?

12.title: Not Because of Our Righteous Acts
12.context: The plea for the desolate sanctuary rests on God's name and compassion, not on Israel's record. Daniel says the ground of his asking out loud, so it cannot be mistaken for a transaction.
12.question: What are you asking God for that you can only ask on the ground of His compassion?

12.title: O Lord, Listen! O Lord, Forgive!
12.context: The prayer ends in three stacked cries, the least composed lines in it. The answer, the next episode shows, had already gone out at the beginning of the petitions.
12.question: When has an answer arrived faster than you could finish asking?

13.title: In Swift Flight, at the Evening Sacrifice
13.context: Gabriel arrives at the hour of the evening sacrifice, which had not been offered in Jerusalem for decades, though Daniel still kept its time in exile. He calls Daniel highly precious, heaven's verdict on the man mid-confession.
13.question: What does it mean to you that heaven dates its answer from the beginning of your petitions?

13.title: Seventy Sevens Decreed
13.context: The seventy sevens answer Daniel's seventy years with a larger measure: six purposes reaching from stopping transgression to anointing the Most Holy Place. Weeks here are sevens, most naturally read as sevens of years, though readers differ on the reckoning.
13.question: Which of the six purposes do you most long to see finished?

13.title: The Messiah Will Be Cut Off
13.context: The count runs from a decree to rebuild Jerusalem toward an anointed prince, and after the sixty-two sevens the anointed one is cut off and the city and sanctuary destroyed again by the people of a prince to come. Which decree begins the count has been debated for centuries.
13.question: What does it do to your reading of history that its center, in this prophecy, is an anointed one being cut off?

13.title: One Week, and the Middle of the Week
13.context: The final seven holds a covenant confirmed and broken at its midpoint and the abomination of desolation in the temple. This is the most interpreted verse in Daniel, and the book gives its architecture without naming its actors.
13.question: How do you hold a prophecy you believe is true without needing to solve every part of it?

13.title: A Calendar Instead of an Explanation
13.context: Daniel asked for his people's return and received the shape of the whole future. The chapter closes without commentary from him, a silence the book will keep until the Tigris vision a decade later.
13.question: What have you asked God for small that He answered large, and how did you carry the difference?

14.title: Three Weeks of Mourning
14.context: The vision is dated to Cyrus's third year, when some exiles had already returned. Daniel, who did not go back, mourns three weeks over a message about a great conflict, with no cause for the mourning named.
14.question: What do you grieve that the people around you have already stopped grieving?

14.title: A Man Dressed in Linen
14.context: The description, linen, gold, beryl, lightning, torches, bronze, echoes Ezekiel's glory and anticipates the risen Christ's appearance in Revelation. Whether this figure is an angel or more is a question readers answer differently; Daniel simply records what he saw.
14.question: When has the nearness of heaven left you with no strength rather than with comfort?

14.title: Left Alone with the Vision
14.context: The men with Daniel felt a terror they could not see the cause of and fled. The word that raises Daniel begins with the same sentence heaven spoke in chapter 9: you are highly precious.
14.question: What sentence from God would you need to hear to stand up trembling and listen anyway?

14.title: Twenty-One Days of Opposition
14.context: The messenger's delay is explained as resistance from the prince of Persia, ended by Michael's help. The chapter is the Bible's clearest window into prayer answered at once and arriving through a contested road.
14.question: How does it change your praying to know the delay may be opposition, not refusal?

14.title: Peace Be with You; Be Strong
14.context: Daniel is touched three times in this chapter, set on his knees, given speech, and given strength. The Book of Truth, from which the next two chapters are read, frames the coming vision as something already written.
14.question: Where do you need to be strengthened before you can hear what God wants to say next?

15.title: Three Kings, a Fourth, and a Mighty King
15.context: Chapter 11 is the longest and most detailed vision in Daniel, tracing Persia's remaining kings, a rich fourth king who stirs up Greece, and a mighty king whose empire splits four ways at his height, Alexander in the usual tracing. The vision names no names throughout.
15.question: What impresses you more in this chapter, how much is told, or that none of it is named?

15.title: Kings of the South and the North
15.context: The long wars are between the Ptolemies of Egypt, the South, and the Seleucids of Syria, the North, in the common historical tracing, with Israel's Beautiful Land on the road between them and repeatedly overrun.
15.question: What is it like to live in the land other powers keep marching through, and where do you see that today?

15.title: A Despicable Person, Seizing by Intrigue
15.context: The despicable king is commonly traced to Antiochus IV, who took the Seleucid throne without royal right. The vision marks him by method: intrigue, deceit, flattery, and a heart set against the holy covenant.
15.question: What methods in a leader tell you what he is, before his policies do?

15.title: The Abomination of Desolation
15.context: Antiochus's desecration of the temple in 167 BC, the daily sacrifice abolished and a pagan altar set up, stands behind these verses in the common tracing, and provoked the Maccabean revolt. The vision's own portrait of God's people is one line: the people who know their God will firmly resist him.
15.question: What would firmly resisting look like for you, in a time when compromise is rewarded?

15.title: Refined, Purified, and Made Spotless
15.context: The wise who instruct many fall by sword and flame and receive only a little help, and the vision interprets their falling as a refinery with a deadline set by God's appointed time, not by their endurance.
15.question: What has a season of falling refined in you that comfort never could?

16.title: The King Who Magnifies Himself
16.context: From verse 36 many readers trace a shift from Antiochus to a later or final king, while others keep the chapter in the second century BC. The vision's own description is of self-deification: no regard for any god, because he magnifies himself above them all.
16.question: Where do you see the worship of power itself, a god of fortresses, honored in your time?

16.title: His End, with No One to Help Him
16.context: The final campaign sweeps through the Beautiful Land and Egypt before the king pitches his tents between the sea and the holy mountain. His obituary is one clause: he meets his end with no one to help him.
16.question: What does the brevity of that ending say about how heaven keeps the records of the proud?

16.title: Many Who Sleep in the Dust Will Awake
16.context: Chapter 12 holds the Old Testament's clearest statement of resurrection, some to everlasting life and others to shame and everlasting contempt, and of the wise shining like stars. The book is then sealed until the time of the end.
16.question: How does the promise that the dust does not keep the wise change how you face death, your own or others'?

16.title: How Long Until the Fulfillment?
16.context: The oath's answer, a time, times, and half a time, matches the horn's grant in chapter 7. Daniel's honesty is the reader's comfort: he heard, and did not understand, and said so to the angel's face.
16.question: What are you willing to keep asking about, even after being told the words are sealed?

16.title: You Will Rest, and Then You Will Arise
16.context: The numbers 1,290 and 1,335 close the visions without unlocking them. The book's last word is personal: Daniel will rest, and arise to his inheritance at the end of the days, the resurrection promised in verse 2 applied to the prophet himself.
16.question: Daniel was sent back to go on his way until the end. What is your way, the ordinary road you are to walk while you wait?
